newsitem.title: TURKEY: Pro-Kurdish figures face 22 years in Turk jails.
newsitem.headline: Pro-Kurdish figures face 22 years in Turk jails.

text.p: Senior members of Turkey's only legal pro-Kurdish political party went on trial on Wednesday in Ankara State Security Court, facing up to 22-1/2 years in prison for alleged separatist activity.

Lawyers for the People's Democracy Party (HADEP) said 18 senior figures, including leader Murat Bozlak, were charged with "leadership of an armed gang". Another 23, mostly rank-and-file members, face up to 15 years under a lesser charge.
Crowds of rights activists, HADEP supporters, family members and western diplomats jammed the courtroom, straining to follow the proceedings.
A similar case threatened to sink Turkey's ambitions for customs union with Europe, granted in late 1995 by a sceptical European Parliament only after Ankara pledged to clean up human rights abuses.

The HADEP defendants were detained in June after masked youths tore down a large Turkish flag adorning a party congress and replaced it with the banner of the outlawed Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) and a poster of its leader Abdullah Ocalan.
Prosecutors say HADEP acts as a front for the PKK, which has waged a bloody 12-year insurgency in predominantly-Kurdish eastern Turkey. More than 20,000 people have died in the fighting.

"It is very clear that this is a political trial," said Sedat Yurtdas, a former MP convicted in the earlier security court trial for links to the PKK. "It is an attempt not to solve the Kurdish problem, rather than to solve it."
HADEP was formed in 1994 after another pro-Kurdish party was closed by the constitutional court for alleged separatism and 13 of its deputies expelled from parliament.
Six Kurdish MPs were later sentenced to jail for links to the PKK insurgents -- a move that angered European public opinion and almost doomed Ankara's bid for the customs union.

Last week, the European Parliament said it would block hundreds of millions of dollars in aid to Turkey for what it said were Ankara's broken promises at the time of customs union to improve the human rights record.

According to the Ankara-based Human Rights Association, 21 people died in extrajudicial executions, in detention or under torture this August, compared with 12 in August of 1995, before the customs accord.
There were 37 cases of police torture in August 1996, against 22 for the same period one year ago, the association said in its latest report.
The authorities deny torture and abuse is endemic in prisons and police stations and say the European Parliament is biased against Turkey.
